title: Mentalization-Based Treatment (MBT) for Borderline Personality Disorder
subtitle: How I Became a Therapy Supervisor, Act 3
text:

By Owen Muir, author

I think every psychiatrist should recognize Borderline Personality Disorder. We all should be able to treat borderline personality disorder. It's 27% of the people who walk into your office. And if you're blind to that, you will do a bad job. No one taught me that. They told me that it's in the book, it's a thing, but no one was saying...

What might Borderline Personality Disorder look like?

Now a person, who's in the hospital for their 30th suicide attempt, that's because—perhaps—they have a personality disorder. It's not only depression. Depression is episodic. It's not bipolar disorder. That has discrete periods of mania. What if they are always like this? They're always impulsive, always suicidal? The suicidal statements and acts can relieves some of their distress, in those with BPD. It can even look like a member of my family.

My sister tried to kill herself twice in one week and was on a liver transplant list. The number of holidays I've spent in emergency rooms with Alison was non-zero. She was among the people with borderline personality disorder for whom substance abuse was also a problem.

She was denied a transplant because she was “a suicide attempt.” She ended up not needing it. She would have died, but her liver regenerated “magically,” so she didn't die. The doctors were perfectly willing to let her die because she tried to kill herself. They decided they shouldn't “waste a good liver”—that is a quote from the attending transplant physician to my family. I'll tell you first what I tell every junior resident or medical student I work with.

Be careful what you say. Someone in the room has whatever you're talking about.

If make a nasty joke about borderline personality disorder, or you refer to a patient as that borderline, with that kind of tone of your voice or that bipolar?

Someone on the team will have that problem too. Play the numbers. They have it, someone in their family has it, or someone very close to them has been through it. They are hearing what you say. When the rubber hits the road, maybe for them or someone close to them, they're not going to let you know.

How I Frame Education about BPD

I'm working to help advocate for more patients and people physicians wanting to treat a serious illness. People with BPD get better!

I start all my talks on BPD as follows:

Okay, who in, who here, y'all have a kid, raise your hand if you'd rather the kid had bipolar disorder or borderline personality disorder…

Okay, bipolar disorder?

Raise your hand.

Everyone's hand goes up.

Borderline personality disorder?

No hands.

While that's happening, everyone with borderline personality disorder in the room, or who fears they might have it, is noticing. They know not to speak up. And they know when they're struggling to not reach out to a colleague for help, because what are they going to think? You're one of those.

I had colleagues coming out to me:

“Owen, can I talk to you?”

Sure. I know what this is going to be about.

“ I have borderline personality disorder. What do I do?”

Therapy vs. Oral medication?

The replication studies on MBT have effect sizes—all subsequent number are in units of “effect size standard deviations”—bigger than basically every drug in psychiatry:

• Plus/minus stimulants in ADHD,

• Better than every drug for depression

• better than every drug for bipolar disorder

• equivalent to ECT in depression

In suicidality MBT is better. It is better than almost anything in medicine. The effect size is 1.26 for reduction of suicidality. Accelerated TMS with SAINT or BRAIN is on par, but anyone can learn MBT without capital investment.

Lithium in bipolar disorder is 0.7 for acute mania. Orders of magnitude different. And it's a psychotherapy!1

Early assessment for those with a personality disorder—the average age of onset is 10.5 years old. Early assessment means people don’t have to spend until age 60 suffering.

Some antipsychotic medicines will give you diabetes. We have perfectly good treatments for BPD that are evidence based that work unbelievably well. They're called therapy.

Polite is the Enemy of the Good

Most people tolerate others who are bullshitting them—because mentalizing allows you to built a model of why you are being lied to that makes sense to you. This has a more common term: “they are being polite.”

Polite is: “lies…that we agree mutually to accept, because all parties agree that the lie is kindness.” We don't get enraged at polite people because politeness is in our mutually agreed—but crucially, implicit—understanding. You are saying “just one moment,” not because that is an exact answer, but because it’s the polite and professional thing to say.

I was interviewing a kid as a demo of MBT, for junior residents who I'm teaching. And and the kid said to me,

“You're like the coolest therapist I've ever talked to. Like, all those other people sound like they're reading from a book.”

I said, “I am, it's just a better book.”

The kid who said I was a good therapist for her, at the beginning of the stay said: “I'm not gonna talk about my trauma.”

This kid spent, six months saying nothing to a therapist every day. She would go into the therapist's office for six months and look at her phone. In one session she tells me everything. There's something to Linehan's biosocial model.

Biological predisposition plus social invalidation, that is the model. That invalidation can be as simple as parent-child mismatch:

Mom, I have to go to the bathroom!

You just went!

It can be much more brutal to outside observers of course: getting violently harmed or assaulted, and being told never to talk about it or “we'll kill you.”

Those are both invalidating experiences.

You take anyone, and you give them enough invalidation—it will create problems with identity, self-direction, empathy, and intimacy. These domains are how I conceive of personality dysfunction.

BPD exists.

Effective therapies like MBT exist, and are potent.

Therapists and Physicians should learn them.

The Frontier Psychiatrists worth the subscription. Do that now.

1Why am I not learning this? Why am I spending time having highly trained analysts not let me know that my patient actually has borderline personality disorder?
